subtopicTitle: Green's theorem — proof sketch, both forms

cards.front: State Green's theorem in circulation form, including all hypotheses.
cards.back: Let C be a positively oriented, piecewise smooth, simple closed curve enclosing a bounded region D with piecewise smooth boundary. If P,Q have continuous partial derivatives on an open set containing D, then ∫_C P dx + Q dy = ∬_D (∂Q/∂x − ∂P/∂y) dA.

cards.front: State Green's theorem in flux (divergence) form.
cards.back: Under the same hypotheses: ∫_C P dy − Q dx = ∬_D (∂P/∂x + ∂Q/∂y) dA. Equivalently, ∫_C F·n ds = ∬_D div F dA.

cards.front: How are the two forms of Green's theorem related by a simple substitution?
cards.back: Replace P by −Q and Q by P in the circulation form to obtain the flux form (and vice versa).

cards.front: Sketch the proof of the circulation form when D is a rectangle [a,b]×[c,d].
cards.back: Write ∬_D (Q_x − P_y) dA = ∫_c^d ∫_a^b Q_x dx dy − ∫_a^b ∫_c^d P_y dy dx. Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to each inner integral; the resulting line integrals telescope to exactly ∫_C P dx + Q dy.

cards.front: Sketch how the proof extends from rectangles to a type-I region D = {(x,y) | a≤x≤b, g(x)≤y≤h(x)}.
cards.back: Decompose the double integral into vertical strips. The inner FTC integrals now run from g(x) to h(x); the resulting boundary terms on the graphs y=g(x), y=h(x) together with the vertical sides at x=a and x=b assemble into the line integral over the whole closed curve C.

cards.front: How is the general case of Green's theorem obtained from the type-I/II cases?
cards.back: Any region whose boundary consists of finitely many piecewise-smooth curves can be decomposed into finitely many type-I or type-II subregions. Internal edges cancel in pairs, leaving only the original outer boundary.

cards.front: What orientation convention must be respected for both forms of Green's theorem?
cards.back: C must be positively oriented (counter-clockwise) with respect to D, so that D lies to the left as one traverses C.
